food.text: Ethiopia's agricultural revolution took place in the third millennium BC. Its early inhabitants had already begun domesticating grains during the Chalcolithic Age (6200-3000 BC), so farming there had deep roots by the start of the Bronze Age.
By the Early Bronze Age, around 3000 BC, people in Ethiopia were domesticating cattle, sheep, goats and donkeys. Herds of these animals became a source of food alongside the grains being grown.
Ethiopian and Eritrean agriculture produced the earliest known use of the seed grass teff, dated between 4000 and 1000 BCE. Teff is still used to make the flatbread injera, also called taita.
According to the source, the agricultural revolution in present-day Ethiopia took place in the third millennium BC. Human settlements there had begun at least in the Late Stone Age.
Pre-Nilotes from Sudan arrived in Ethiopia about the third millennium BC. They were mostly farmers who developed the cultivation of sorghum and tuberous plants such as enset and yams.
Pre-Nilotes arrived in Ethiopia about the third millennium BC and were mostly agriculturalists. They developed the cultivation of sorghum and tuberous plants like enset and yams.
The rock paintings of Hararghe and Eritrea suggest that by the late third millennium BC, rudimentary agriculture had begun in many parts of western Ethiopia.
The development of plough-based agriculture in early Ethiopia may imply that cattle were domesticated around the same time as grains. If so, farmers may have used cattle to work their fields.

The Pre-Nilotes who grew sorghum, enset and yams are said to be ancestors of peoples settled in western Ethiopia today, namely the Berta, Gumuz and Koma. Their early farming traditions are tied to the western edge of the country.

art.text: In the 2nd millennium BCE, people in the eastern Turkana region of northwestern Kenya raised Namoratunga, also called Monolith Circles. These megaliths were constructed as burials.

Around Kassala, on the border between Sudan and Eritrea, the Gash Group flourished from around 3000 to 1500 BCE, with Mahal Teglinos as its leading site. Its remains include funerary steles, architecture and standardized pottery, evidence of a fairly complex society.

art.text: The Gash Group was a crossroads for trade between Kerma, the Red Sea and the Ethiopian Highlands. It was contemporaneous with the Kerma culture in Nubia, so its potters and builders worked within a wide network of contacts.

art.text: The ancient Egyptian conquest of Kerma around 1550 BCE broke the Gash Group's trade crossroads role. Groups with Middle Nubian ceramics then settled the region, bringing a different pottery tradition to the area around Kassala.

literature.text: Ancient Egyptian textual records sometimes called the Land of Punt 'Ta netjer', meaning 'Land of the God'. This name reflected how Egyptian writings treated the region, located southeast of Egypt in East Africa, as an almost sacred and legendary place.

In Egypt's Twelfth Dynasty, trade with the Land of Punt was celebrated in popular literature, appearing in the Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor. This shows how significant Punt, in East Africa, had become in Egyptian storytelling.

Inside Queen Hatshepsut's mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, relief sculptures and texts recount an expedition to the Land of Punt, described as an exotic country on the Red Sea coast. The same temple walls also recite the tale of the pharaoh's divine birth.

Egyptian records indicate that trade with the Land of Punt had already begun by around 2500 BCE or even earlier. This makes Punt one of the earliest foreign lands documented in ancient Egyptian written sources.

An inscription in the Wadi Hammamat records that King Mentuhotep III sent an expedition of 3,000 men to the Land of Punt during the eighth year of his reign. The mission was commanded by the steward Henenu.

Egyptian accounts described the peoples of Punt as semi-mythical 'horizon dwellers'. This phrase, preserved in Egyptian textual records, captures how remote and legendary the East African land seemed to Egyptian writers.

The Wadi Hammamat inscription describes Henenu's expedition leaving Coptos toward the Red Sea. The men dug 12 wells for future expeditions and cleared the region of rebels. They returned from Punt with incense, gum and perfumes, and quarried the Wadi Hammamat for stones.

The Wadi Hammamat inscription suggests Henenu's expedition to Punt may have departed from a Red Sea port possibly identified as Mersa Gawasis. The inscription itself leaves this identification as an open question.

science.text: According to the Greek historian Agatharchides, during the prosperous Old Kingdom period between the 30th and 25th centuries BC, Egyptian ships sailed the Red Sea as far as the myrrh-country of Punt in the Horn of Africa. This shows early Egyptian seafaring technology reaching the region for trade.

Between about 3000 and 1500 BCE, the Gash Group centered at Kassala, on the border of Sudan and Eritrea, developed standardized pottery and administrative devices as part of a growing, complex society. It served as a crossroads linking the Kerma culture, the Red Sea, and the Ethiopian Highlands.
science.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

science.text: Between about 3800 and 3000 BCE, the Butana Group living east of the Atbara River made mace-heads from porphyry stone carried roughly 300 kilometres from the northeast. These imported stone tools were associated with wealthy burials, showing early technology tied to social status.
science.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

politics.text: Around Kassala, on the border between Sudan and Eritrea, the Gash Group flourished from about 3000 to 1500 BCE. It was contemporaneous with the Kerma culture in Nubia. Its leading site was Mahal Teglinos, and it is thought to have had five levels of social hierarchy.
politics.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

politics.text: The Gash Group served as a crossroad for trade between Kerma, the Red Sea, and the Ethiopian Highlands. The ancient Egyptian conquest of Kerma around 1550 BCE broke this practice. Groups of people with Middle Nubian ceramics then settled the region.
politics.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

politics.text: Egyptian traders from about 3000 BC referred to the lands south of Nubia, or Kush, as Punt and Yam. Isotope analysis of mummified Egyptian baboons suggests they came from an area covering modern Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Somalia. This has led to the hypothesis that Punt was a kingdom in the Horn of Africa.

The Greek geographer Agatharchides recorded that during the prosperous Old Kingdom, between the 30th and 25th centuries BC, Egypt kept its river-routes in order. Egyptian ships sailed the Red Sea as far as the myrrh-country. This points to organized state-backed contact with Punt.

After Egypt's conquest of Kerma around 1550 BCE ended the Gash Group's role as a trade crossroads, people bringing Middle Nubian ceramic traditions settled the Kassala region. Their arrival marked a shift in the pottery-making traditions used there.
politics.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

politics.text: The Gash Group left strong evidence of social complexity, including settlement patterns, funerary steles, administrative devices, architecture, and standardized pottery. It became more socially stratified over time and may have been a chiefdom. However, no definitive evidence of this has been uncovered.
politics.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

politics.text: During the Fourth Egyptian Dynasty (2789–2767 BC), a Puntite is mentioned as being in the service of the son of Cheops, the builder of the Great Pyramid. It is an early sign of people from Punt living within the Egyptian royal circle.

Hatshepsut's temple reliefs present her envoy, Chancellor Nehsi, as extracting tribute from Punt. In reality his expedition was a simple trading mission to a well-established trading post. The reliefs say Punt was then ruled by King Parahu and Queen Ati.

J. H. Breasted suggested that early trade between Egypt and Punt could have moved overland down the Nile and its tributaries, namely the Blue Nile and the Atbara. Such a route would have linked Egyptian rulers to the Horn without depending on sea voyages.

culture.text: Human settlement in present-day Ethiopia began at least in the Late Stone Age. The agricultural revolution then took place there in the third millennium BC, changing how people lived and fed themselves.
New ethnic, cultural and linguistic identities emerged in Ethiopia around 2000 to 1000 BC. They belonged to Afroasiatic speakers (Semitic, Cushitic and Omotic) and to Nilo-Saharan speakers.

The Gash Group, centred on Mahal Teglinos near Kassala on the border of Sudan and Eritrea, dates from around 3000 to 1500 BCE. It was a crossroad for trade between Kerma in Nubia, the Red Sea and the Ethiopian Highlands.
culture.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

culture.text: Rock paintings of human and animal figures in the Hararghe region and Eritrea illustrate the domestication of cattle. They also show the crafting of pottery, hand axes, hoes and grinding stones, suggesting rudimentary agriculture had begun in many parts of western Ethiopia by the late third millennium BC.

Independent linguistic analysis shows Semitic speakers were present in Ethiopia by at least 2000 BC. Proto-Ethiopians are thought to have spoken Afroasiatic languages in the third millennium BC, probably originating in the Eastern Sahara after its desertification.

The Gash Group shows much evidence of social complexity, including funerary steles, administrative devices, architecture and standardized pottery. It became more socially stratified over time and is thought to have had five levels of social hierarchy.
culture.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

culture.text: Limestone caves in Dire Dawa hold evidence of stone hand tools, blade instruments and drawings. They are part of the record of early crafting and art in Ethiopia.
The Central Cushites spoke the dialect cluster called Agaw and occupied northwestern Ethiopia. They are known for the plow cultivation of cereal grains.
Comparatively little research has been done in the Eritrean-Ethiopian highlands. The earliest groups identified there date to the 3rd and 2nd millennium BCE, near Mekelle in Ethiopia.
culture.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

culture.text: Recent findings suggest that crafting was introduced to Ethiopia from Sudan via the Blue Nile Valley. This points to early cultural links between the Ethiopian region and its northern neighbour.
